joints.name: Butt Joint
joints.summary: A butt joint places two members edge to edge in the same plane — the simplest joint to draw and the one that most often needs edge preparation to reach full penetration.
joints.meta_description: Butt joint welding explained: edge preparation, groove angles, root opening, when a square edge works and when you need a V, U or J groove.
joints.geometry: Two members lying in the same plane, joined along their abutting edges.
joints.prep: Square edge up to roughly 3/16 in; single-V above that; double-V, U or J on thick plate to cut filler volume and balance distortion.
joints.strength: A full-penetration butt joint develops the full strength of the base metal, which is why it is specified on pressure and structural work.
characteristics: The only common joint that can be made with no weld metal above the surface of the members.
Needs edge preparation above about 3/16 in to reach the root with the arc.
Root opening and land thickness control how much penetration the root pass achieves.
Distortion is angular: the joint pulls closed as the weld cools, so tack sequence and a slight preset matter.
Backing bars, backing welds or back gouging are the usual routes to full penetration when only one side is accessible.
applications: Sheet metal panels joined edge to edge

faqs.q: Do butt joints need edge preparation?
faqs.a: Below about 3/16 in a square-edge butt joint welds through without preparation. Above that the arc cannot reach the root, so the edges are bevelled into a V, U or J groove.

faqs.q: What is the strongest welding joint?
faqs.a: A full-penetration butt joint develops the full strength of the base metal, which makes it the strongest joint configuration. The trade-off is that it demands the most preparation and the most careful fit-up.

faqs.q: What is a root opening in a butt joint?
faqs.a: The gap between the two members at the bottom of the groove before welding. It gives the arc access to the root; too little causes lack of penetration, too much causes burn-through.

faqs.q: Why do butt joints distort?
faqs.a: Weld metal shrinks as it cools. On a single-V joint most of the weld sits near the top surface, so the joint pulls angularly closed. Presetting the members open, alternating passes, or using a double-V balances it.

joints.name: Lap Joint
joints.summary: A lap joint overlaps two members and welds along the exposed edges — no edge preparation, forgiving fit-up, and the cheapest joint to fabricate.
joints.meta_description: Lap joint welding explained: fillet weld sizing, overlap distance, single vs double fillet, plug and spot weld alternatives, and fatigue limitations.
joints.geometry: Two members overlapping face to face, with fillet welds along one or both exposed edges.
joints.prep: None required beyond cleaning. Overlap is typically three to five times the thinner member's thickness.
joints.strength: Loaded in shear rather than tension. A double-fillet lap joint carries substantially more load than a single fillet and avoids the bending that a single weld introduces.
characteristics: Requires no edge preparation, which makes it the fastest joint to fabricate.
Very tolerant of poor fit-up and cutting inaccuracy.
A single-fillet lap joint loads the weld eccentrically and tends to peel; two fillets are preferred where load matters.
Creates a crevice between the members that traps moisture — a corrosion concern in wet or marine service.
Poor fatigue performance relative to a butt joint because of the sharp stress concentration at the weld toe.
applications: Automotive body panels, usually spot welded
General repair where fit-up is rough

faqs.q: How much overlap does a lap joint need?
faqs.a: A common rule is three to five times the thickness of the thinner member. Less than that and the fillet welds interact; more adds weight without adding strength.

faqs.q: Should a lap joint be welded on both sides?
faqs.a: For anything carrying load, yes. A single fillet loads the joint eccentrically, which bends it and encourages peeling. Two fillets balance the load path.

faqs.q: Are lap joints as strong as butt joints?
faqs.a: No. A full-penetration butt joint develops the full base metal strength; a lap joint's capacity is limited by the shear area of its fillet welds and it performs poorly in fatigue.

faqs.q: Can you use plug welds instead of fillets on a lap joint?
faqs.a: Yes. Plug or slot welds through the top member are used where the edges are not accessible or where a flush outer surface is wanted, and they are common in automotive work.

joints.name: T-Joint
joints.summary: A T-joint sets one member perpendicular to the face of another, and it is normally filleted on both sides — the most common joint in structural fabrication.
joints.meta_description: T-joint welding explained: fillet leg size and throat, single vs double fillet, when full penetration needs a bevel or J groove, and lamellar tearing.
joints.geometry: One member meeting the face of another at approximately 90 degrees, away from its edge.
joints.prep: None for fillet welds. Full-penetration T-joints require a single or double bevel or J groove on the upright member.
joints.strength: Fillet capacity is governed by the throat, which for an equal-leg fillet is the leg size multiplied by 0.707. Doubling the leg size does not double the strength economically — two smaller fillets usually beat one large one.
characteristics: The workhorse joint of structural steel: beams to columns, stiffeners to webs, brackets to plates.
Double fillets are standard because a single fillet bends the joint under load.
Full penetration requires bevelling the upright member, usually shown as a bevel-groove or J-groove symbol combined with a fillet.
Puts through-thickness stress on the horizontal member, which raises the risk of lamellar tearing on thick plate.
Fillet size is often overspecified: a 5/16 in fillet contains more than twice the metal of a 3/16 in fillet.
applications: Tank and vessel nozzles and supports

faqs.q: What size fillet weld does a T-joint need?
faqs.a: It depends on the load and the governing code, but a common practical minimum is a fillet leg roughly equal to the thickness of the thinner member, up to the code's maximum. Oversizing wastes filler and adds distortion without proportional strength.

faqs.q: What is the throat of a fillet weld?
faqs.a: The shortest distance from the root to the face of the weld — for an equal-leg fillet, the leg size multiplied by 0.707. The throat, not the leg, is what carries the load.

faqs.q: When does a T-joint need a groove weld?
faqs.a: When the design calls for complete joint penetration. The upright member is bevelled into a single or double bevel or J groove, and the symbol usually combines the groove with a fillet to give the finished weld its contour.

faqs.q: What is lamellar tearing?
faqs.a: A crack that runs parallel to the surface of the base plate, caused by weld shrinkage pulling on the plate through its thickness. It is a risk on thick T-joints with large welds, and is addressed with lower-strength filler, buttering layers and plate specified for through-thickness properties.

joints.name: Corner Joint
joints.summary: A corner joint brings two members together at their edges to form an L, and unlike a T-joint the upright lands on the end of the other member rather than in the middle of it.
joints.meta_description: Corner joint welding explained: open vs closed corner, single and double fillets, groove preparation for full penetration, and burn-through control.
joints.geometry: Two members meeting at approximately 90 degrees at their edges, forming an L in section.
joints.prep: None for a filleted corner. Open corners with a groove preparation are used where full penetration or a flush outside corner is required.
joints.strength: Depends heavily on configuration. A closed corner with a single inside fillet is weak in the opening direction; welding both inside and outside, or using a groove weld, transforms it.
characteristics: Easy to confuse with a T-joint on a drawing — the difference is that the upright sits at the END of the other member.
The outside corner is prone to burn-through because there is little metal to absorb the heat.
Welding only the inside corner leaves the joint able to open under load; outside welds or a groove preparation fix that.
Very common on box sections, frames and enclosures where two faces meet.
Distortion pulls the included angle closed, so tacking and sequence matter more than on a T-joint.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a corner joint and a T-joint?
faqs.a: Where the upright lands. In a T-joint it meets the face of the other member somewhere in the middle; in a corner joint it meets the end, so the two members form an L.

faqs.q: Should you weld the inside or outside of a corner joint?
faqs.a: Both where the joint carries load. An inside fillet alone lets the corner open under load. The outside weld, or a groove preparation welded from outside, is what closes the load path.

faqs.q: Why does my corner joint keep burning through?
faqs.a: There is little base metal at an outside corner to conduct heat away. Drop the amperage, speed up travel, or use a smaller electrode. On thin material, backstepping and skip welding also help.

faqs.q: How do you get full penetration on a corner joint?
faqs.a: Bevel one or both members into an open corner preparation, which lets the root pass reach the joint root, and back weld or back gouge if both sides are accessible.

joints.name: Edge Joint
joints.summary: An edge joint lays two members face to face and welds along their common edge — a light-duty joint used to join flanges and sheet edges, not to carry load.
joints.meta_description: Edge joint welding explained: where it fits, why it is not a load-bearing joint, autogenous welding on sheet, and the alternatives for structural work.
joints.geometry: Two parallel or nearly parallel members with their edges aligned, welded along that common edge.
joints.prep: Usually none. Thicker members may be bevelled into a V or J groove along the edge.
joints.strength: Low. The weld is not in the load path in any useful direction, so edge joints are used for sealing, alignment and light assembly rather than for transferring structural load.
characteristics: Among the easiest joints to weld: the two edges sit right at the top of the puddle.
Frequently welded autogenously — fusing the edges together with no filler metal at all.
Not a load-bearing configuration; the weld carries very little in tension or shear.
Used to seal seams, join flanges and hold light assemblies in alignment.
On thin sheet, it is one of the few joints where a TIG torch alone with no filler gives a clean, finished result.
applications: Tanks and ducting where the joint seals rather than carries load

faqs.q: Is an edge joint strong?
faqs.a: No. It is a light-duty configuration used for sealing, alignment and assembly. Where load has to be transferred, a butt, lap or T-joint is used instead.

faqs.q: Can you weld an edge joint without filler metal?
faqs.a: Yes — on thin sheet, the two edges can be fused autogenously with a TIG torch. It is one of the few joints where that works cleanly.

faqs.q: When would you use an edge joint?
faqs.a: Joining flanges, sealing sheet metal seams, and light assembly work where the weld holds parts in position rather than carrying structural load.

faqs.q: Does an edge joint need preparation?
faqs.a: Usually none. On thicker members the edge may be bevelled into a V or J groove so the weld reaches the full thickness rather than just fusing the top.
